Thursday: High pressure continues to build over the Inland 
Northwest continues to keep things warm and dry. Temperatures today 
will warm into the mid to high 90s, bringing a Moderate chance of 
HeatRisk to the Inland Northwest. All those sensitive to heat-
related illnesses should make sure they have adequate access to 
cooling and hydration, and some systems and industries will be 
impacted. Very warm high temperatures, relative humidity values 12-
20 percent, and sufficient mixing will result in elevated fire 
weather concerns over the Cascades, especially for already 
established wildfires. 

Friday through Sunday: Models finally look to be converging on 
timing of an incoming cold front bringing gusty winds and isolated 
to scattered thunderstorms to the region. Ahead of the cold front 
passage on Saturday, temperatures on Friday warm into the high 90s 
with triple digits expected in the lower Basin and Lewiston areas. 
This has led to widespread Major HeatRisk values, which indicates 
that anyone without adequate cooling and hydration as well as 
health systems and industries could see impacts. To reflect 
this, a Heat Advisory has been issued for nearly all parts of 
the region tomorrow from 11 AM to 10 PM. Additionally, low 
temperatures in the 60s and 70s will provide little overnight 
relief. 

Friday night into Saturday, moisture advection ahead of the frontal 
passage will raise PWATs to 125 to 150 percent of normal. On 
Saturday into Sunday, the arrival of the cold front reinforced by a 
40-50kt 500mb jet and warm overnight and daytime temperatures will 
create a favorable environment for isolated to scattered 
thunderstorms across the Cascades and northern mountains areas. 
While these showers will initially start out as isolated in nature, 
as higher PWATs increase in coverage, thunderstorms will become more 
scattered in nature, especially into later Saturday morning. With 
PWATs near 1 inch and DCAPE values 500 J/kg and higher, main impacts 
with these storms look to be heavy downpours, gusty outflow winds 
near 40 to 50 mph, and lightning. Steep terrain and burn scars will 
need to be monitored for any heavy rainfall rates. This threat will 
move eastward across the forecast area through the day, and Saturday 
night into Sunday morning the ID Panhandle has the same chances at 
seeing isolated to scattered thunderstorms. To reflect these 
critical fire weather conditions, Fire Weather Watches have been 
issued. For the Cascades and northern mountains, the Fire Weather 
Watch has been issued from Saturday morning through Sunday morning. 
For the ID Panhandle, a Fire Weather Watch has been issued from 
Saturday afternoon through Sunday morning. 

Additionally, in the afternoon and evening, winds will increase with 
the cold frontal passage, particularly across the Columbia Basin. 
There is a 40 percent chance and higher for most locations in the 
region to see wind gusts higher than 30 mph on Saturday night. Areas 
that will see the highest gusts include the Lewiston, Moses Lake, 
Wenatchee, and Waterville Plateau areas. These areas have a 40 
percent chance of seeing wind gusts 35 mph or higher. This will 
bring critical fire weather conditions to the area. A Fire Weather 
Watch has been issued for the basin, Palouse, and Spokane areas from 
Saturday afternoon through Saturday evening. Potential impacts from 
these winds include rapid spreading of wildfires alongside blowing 
objects and difficulties driving, especially for high profile 
vehicles. 

Initially, models had the low moving out of the area quicker, but 
are now in better agreement that the low will linger over the state 
of Washington through Sunday before moving out of the area Sunday 
night into Monday. This will result in impacts from the cold front 
being seen into Sunday afternoon. In the morning, the northern Idaho 
Panhandle will continue to see isolated to scattered thunderstorms. 
One thing to keep a close eye on is the extent of the thunderstorms 
post cold frontal passage on Sunday morning. Some models are showing 
enough lingering instability throughout Spokane that it may need to 
be added into the Saturday into Sunday Fire Weather Watch. 
Additionally, residual wind gusts around 15-20 mph will linger 
throughout the Cascade gaps, Okanogan Valley, Waterville Plateau, 
Columbia Basin, Spokane/CdA, and Palouse areas through late Sunday 
afternoon. These winds will result in continued elevated fire 
weather conditions. 

A significant cooldown due to the cold front will be observed 
Saturday into Sunday, with high temperatures dropping nearly ten 
degrees. This cooldown will result in temperatures being a couple 
degrees below normal on Sunday. By Sunday evening, precipitation
chances across the region drop down to near zero.
